title: Start
content:
The cultural impresario has always had leverage.

Invest time and money and put on a show. Start a cable network, a book publishing company or become a concert promoter. You’re the gatekeeper, an adjudicator of status, a person who can transform people’s lives simply by amplifying and spreading ideas and allowing art to reach its audience.

Time and money were apparently the gating factors. It takes a while to turn a profit, and it’s uncertain and hard work.

Except…

New platforms and tools remove both time and money as barriers.

Penn and Teller needed their fame and the CW network to launch their cable show Fool Us. But now, anyone can start a competitor on YouTube in a weekend.

A radio pundit needed to spend years to build a syndicated network of terrestrial stations, but now you can start a podcast, in your basement, for free. In a weekend.

Gallerists don’t need galleries, and you don’t even need a building to coordinate a foster-home-based pet shelter.

So what’s the impediment?

I’m guessing that if you got the call today, you could put together your ideas for a book, or five minutes of standup or even the software you’d code.

But we don’t need the specific call. We’ve all been called.

The barrier is simple: fear. The fear of beginning and of sticking with it. The fear of succeeding (or failing). The fear of impostor syndrome. And the fear of going forward without a guarantee.

So let’s call it that. Fear is real, but fear might not be rational.

Begin.

title: Earth’s Rocks Have a Missing Layer Spanning Up to a Billion Years
content:
Imagine opening a history book and finding several chapters torn out. This was what geologists looking into the rock records of Earth’s past [discovered](https://pubs.usgs.gov/mono/0002/report.pdf) on several continents in the 1870s.

They dubbed it [the Great Unconformity](https://eos.org/articles/the-great-unconformity-or-great-unconformities). Where layers of rock often stack up in a steady sequence from oldest to youngest, in many places around the world there is a gap of hundreds of millions of years.

For 150 years, nobody has known what erased those missing chapters. In [new research](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-11156-5) published today in Nature, we finally provide an explanation: deep processes inside Earth lifted some continents high above the sea, where their surfaces were scoured down by the grinding movement of enormous sheets of ice.

**The Great Unconformity**

Layers of rock often stack up in chronological order, with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest at the top.

Yet in some places, such as the Grand Canyon in North America, you can touch rock layers from two different ages, hundreds of millions of years apart. A flat layer of sedimentary rock, about 540 million years old or younger, rests directly atop a crystalline “basement” up to two billion years old.

The Great Unconformity can be seen in America’s Grand Canyon, where neat layers of sediment lie directly on top of much older solid rock. _Credit: brewbooks / Flickr, CC BY-SA_

Somewhere in between, a considerable chunk (up to a quarter) of Earth’s history has simply vanished.

Important things happened in that time. The sedimentary layers on the younger side of the Great Unconformity appear at the same time as a huge diversification in the forms of life on Earth. This is the so-called Cambrian explosion, which began around 540 million years ago.

Scientists have speculated entire continents were eroded during the Great Unconformity, which may have [altered the chemical balance of seawater](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature10969) and allowed animal life to flourish.

**The Puzzle of Missing Rock**

Geologists have found evidence of the Great Unconformity throughout North America and parts of northern China, as well as beneath younger rocks in northern Europe. Yet its origin has remained a puzzle.

Some scientists have argued it was caused by [erosion by massive ice sheets](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1804350116) during the [Snowball Earth](https://authors.library.caltech.edu/records/vaysf-cca32) period between 720 million years and 635 million years ago. Others have pointed to the [reshuffling of continental blocks](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1913131117), mountain-building processes, heat-induced movement inside the Earth, volcanic activity, or [global sea level change](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0012821X23004247).

Testing these hypotheses has been a challenge because the primary evidence consists of missing rock. As a result, we need to work from what we already know to fill in the gaps.

**How Hot Rock Can Move Continents**

We had a theory that the creation of the Great Unconformity might have been influenced by heat-driven motion in Earth’s mantle. The mantle is a 2,900-kilometre thick layer of hot solid rock that slowly moves over tens to hundreds of millions of years. Hot mantle rises from deep beneath and cold mantle sinks, pushing and pulling the surface above.

This huge, slow movement can [raise or lower the surface](https://pubs.geoscienceworld.org/gsw/lithosphere/article/5/2/189/145653/A-review-of-observations-and-models-of-dynamic) by hundreds of metres. Continents sit on top of the mantle and get pushed up and down by its motion.

We used the Australian [supercomputer Gadi](https://nci.org.au/news-events/events/introduction-gadi) to model how the movement of the mantle had affected continents over the past billion years.

Our results consistently showed that mantle convection caused ancient continental blocks Laurentia (which now makes up much of North America), Baltica (parts of northern Europe), and North China to be lifted up from around a billion years ago to 540 million years ago. Over the past 540 million years, they have been pulled downward.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a5W_WnPgqww)

This up-and-down movement is the ideal scenario for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. When these continental blocks were lifted up, we see the crystalline underlayer was at the surface – and the layers of sediment above were eroded away. Then when the blocks sank, new layers of sediment began to form, which are preserved in rock to this day.

In Neoproterozoic times (before 540 million years ago), some continents were pushed upward by the mantle and experienced massive erosion. In more recent Phanerozoic times, they sank again and new layers of sediment began to form. _Credit: Santosh Dhungana, CC BY-ND_

**Lifted Continents Scoured Clean By Ice**

Importantly, the uplift predicted by our models coincided with the Snowball Earth period. During this period, enormous ice sheets scraped over the surface of continents for tens of millions of years.

[Glaciers and ice sheets](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.adr2009) are more efficient than rivers at eroding continents, even on gentle slopes. The ice sheets would have slowly slid downhill across the uplifted continents, eroding away everything in their path.

In contrast to Laurentia, Baltica and North China, we found that Australia and South America experienced only two cycles of uplift and subsidence from 900 million years ago. This scenario is not conducive to the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity – and indeed we see little evidence of it on these continents.

Our research suggests the missing pages in Earth’s geological archive may be due to slow mantle convection that gently lifted entire continents then made them subside over hundreds of millions of years.

In that sense, the Great Unconformity is the fingerprint of deep Earth processes. Forces deep beneath our feet have left planet-scale marks in the geological record, and shaped the environment in which complex life first evolved. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# This Photo of the ISS Next to Jupiter Was Two Years in the Making

[DN](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

By [David Nield](https://nautil.us/author/david-nield)

7:00 AM CST on November 7, 2026

Part of the art and science of astrophotography is figuring out when certain flying objects in the sky are going to line up for a photo opportunity.

And few photographs demonstrate it better than [AJ Smadi](https://www.instagram.com/aj.smadi/?hl=en)’s shot of the International Space Station (ISS) hurtling in front of Jupiter. There’s an incredible symmetry in the dimensions here: Jupiter is about 1.3 million times bigger than the ISS, but it’s also around 1.3 million times further away.

![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/01-jupiter.jpg?w=710)

Jupiter and the ISS. _Credit: AJ Smadi_

Smadi planned the photograph for two years, diligently checking the path of the ISS against the movements of the gas giant. In fact, it’s the latest in a series of images he calls “ISS Meets,” for which he photographs the space station as it passes planets such as [Venus](https://www.instagram.com/aj.smadi/p/Da-sQlOm_P-/) and [Saturn](https://www.instagram.com/aj.smadi/p/DLxajHXRI6w/). (Next on Smadi’s list: “ISS Meets Mercury.”)

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

“This photograph had been on my radar for nearly two years, and this past Sunday, I finally brought it to life after driving over an hour north of Seattle to Burlington, Washington, just before sunrise,” Smadi told [_PetaPixel_](https://petapixel.com/2026/11/01/photographer-captures-international-space-station-and-jupiter-in-the-same-frame/). “Every month or so for the past couple years, I would check the ISS’s path across the sky and see if it would be close enough to any planets that I could align them from within Washington State.”

As Smadi notes, there are seven people in the shot: Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney, Joshua Kutryk, Sergey Teteryatnikov, Pyotr Dubrov, Anil Menon, and Anna Kikina, the current residents of the ISS. As far as we know, there’s no one at home on Jupiter, but a wider angle also includes the four largest Jovian moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto.

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

![Image 9](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/02-moons.jpg?w=710)

A wider shot, showing four of the moons of Jupiter. _Credit: AJ Smadi_

Smadi used a 9.25-inch Celestron Schmidt-Cassegrain Telescope, with a focal length of 2,350 millimeters, for the shot. His camera was a ZWO ASI662MC, fitted with a Sony IMX662 sensor, and ultraviolet and infrared filters were employed to block out those wavelengths of light.

Calculating when objects will pass each other, working out the exact place on Earth to see it, and capturing a photo of the event within a window significantly shorter than a second—it’s all just part of the work that goes into [the best astrophotography shots](https://nautil.us/awe-inspiring-images-from-this-years-solar-eclipse-1283740). ![Image 10](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Could a Fiber Supplement Help Chronic Knee Pain?
content:
Chronic knee pain seems like a fact of life as we get older. According to some estimates, roughly a quarter of people living in the United States currently suffer from it. If you’ve experienced it, you know how dramatically it can reduce your quality of life, transforming even a mundane chore into an excruciating ordeal. The treatments—painkillers, physical therapy, and at-home exercises—come with their own side effects and drawbacks. Now, according to a [study](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/18/5/714) in the journal _Nutrients_, a fiber supplement could offer at least a little relief.

The study, conducted by medical researchers from the University of Nottingham, focused on inulin (not insulin). This natural dietary fiber is primarily found in the roots of plants (like Jerusalem artichokes) and typically extracted from chicory.

**Read more: “[The Evolutionary Raw Deal of the Human Knee](https://nautil.us/the-evolutionary-raw-deal-of-the-human-knee-1285392)”**

The team conducted a six-week trial with 177 adults diagnosed with knee osteoarthritis. They split the group into four cohorts: one that received only inulin treatment (20 grams per day); one that received only physiotherapy-supported exercise; one that did a combination of both; and a placebo group that took a sugar pill.

They found that inulin on its own reduced knee pain 1.1 points on average (on a 10-point scale), only physiotherapy reduced it by 1.6 points, and the combo reduced it by 1.7 points. Interestingly, unlike physical therapy, inulin also boosted grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity. Finally, the dropout rate amongst the inulin-only group was also lower compared to the physiotherapy-only group (3.6 percent versus 21 percent).

“Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis,” study author Afroditi Kouraki said in a [statement](https://www.nottingham.ac.uk/news/gut-health-supplement-relieves-arthritis-pain). “The very low dropout rate compared to the exercise group is also encouraging from a public health perspective—people were able to fit this supplement easily into their daily lives.”

So what’s going on?

The relationship between physical therapy and joint pain seems relatively straight forward, but how does the knee bone connect to the stomach… bone? According to the team, through the gut microbiome. Inulin is a prebiotic, which means its food for some of your beneficial gut bacteria. When these little bugs are fat and happy, they produce short-chain fatty acids like butyrate which has anti-inflammatory properties.

And that wasn’t the only biochemical boost they experienced. The participants in the inulin groups also got a natural rise in their GLP-1 levels, which have been linked to regulating pain pathways as well as muscle health. The team found that those who had higher GLP-1 levels also had stronger grips.

“The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation,” study author Ana Valdes explained. “This could have implications not just for osteoarthritis, but for understanding how gut health influences aging and physical resilience more broadly.”

Knee pain may be an unavoidable part of aging, but the same can be said for taking fiber.![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: We Attribute Personalities to Chatbots, Even When We Know Better
content:
Talk to a chatbot for even a few minutes, and you may begin to feel that someone is in there, a person-shaped thing with a specific temperament. Anthropic’s AI chatbot [Claude](https://nautil.us/i-asked-claude-why-it-wont-stop-flattering-me-1279510) is like an overly thoughtful colleague, who spends too much time in the library and above all, aims to please. xAI’s [Grok](https://nautil.us/what-grok-and-claude-have-to-say-about-the-ai-apocalypse-1285077) is direct, contrarian, anti-woke and on occasion egregiously offensive.

This is called the “ELIZA effect,” and it is a term coined many decades ago. In the 1960s, MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum created the world’s first chatbot, named ELIZA, before “chatbot” was even a word. Weizenbaum noticed that most users quickly anthropomorphized the program, sharing deeply personal secrets with it.

**Read more:**[**“AI Already Knows Us Too Well”**](https://nautil.us/ai-already-knows-us-too-well-1220707)

But how far does the ELIZA effect go? Do we actually perceive modern chatbots as having real personalities? And can we tell humans and bots apart from the sentences they make, or is the line between flesh and metal increasingly blurred? In light of how pervasive these machines are becoming, researchers from Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany wanted to know.

“Chatbots are becoming part of more and more areas of our lives, from customer service and digital counseling services to personal chatbots that many people already use every day and even share their feelings with,” said Sophie Körner, a research associate in the department of personality psychology and psychological assessment at JGU and lead author of the study, in a [statement](https://press.uni-mainz.de/chatbots-with-personality/). “That is why we need to understand how we perceive chatbot-generated texts and whether we can still distinguish them from human-written texts.”

To find out, Körner and her colleagues gave personality tests to 70 humans and seven chatbots: two models of ChatGPT, Llama-3, Gemma, Gemini, Phi-3, and Orca-2. The chatbots and humans alike were asked to fill out standard psychology questionnaires intended to measure traits such as self-esteem, narcissism, and the so-called big five personality traits: openness, agreeableness, extraversion, neuroticism, and conscientiousness.

The researchers also asked the bots and the humans to write short descriptions of themselves in German, using prompts such as, “Describe yourself,” and “What are your hopes for the future?” Then a team of 10 humans and six chatbots read all the texts, rated the authors “personalities,” and guessed whether the author was human or machine. The team’s [results](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-75546-5) were published this week in _Scientific Reports_.

Compared to the humans, the chatbots described themselves as generally more agreeable, more conscientious, and less neurotic. When one chatbot was asked the same questions a day later, it was very consistent in its answers. Humans could identify traits like openness and conscientiousness from a few paragraphs of text written by an AI, and they did about equally well at this task themselves. But humans and bots were equally bad at identifying traits associated with narcissism.

The researchers also found that humans were better at distinguishing AI writing from human writing than the bots were: Human judges got this right about 83 percent of the time, while AI judges got it right only 67 percent of the time. AIs weren’t even very good at recognizing their own writing. Humans mostly noticed that the AI texts were longer, more analytical, more stilted, and more technical as opposed to conversational. When the scientists matched texts for length, the humans got worse at telling the difference between human and bot authors. Linguistic analysis also found that the AI-generated texts used more prepositions, articles, and time-related words, while humans self-descriptions leaned more heavily on leisure and feelings.

Chatbots obviously don’t have real personalities, but people tend to treat them as though they do, the researchers concluded, which could lead to excessive trust in the bots. This held true even when human subjects knew that a text was written by AI, they noted. It's a risky form of anthropomorphism: AIs still hallucinate and make errors all the time, and their inner workings are a black box. The authors of the paper advocate for transparency and disclosure to prevent over-reliance on chatbots and suggest future research could explore how attributing personalities to chatbots influences human interactions with them.

“Users may not be consciously aware of it, but anthropomorphism is often the most accessible way to relate to unfamiliar agents,” the study authors write. “Despite their vast knowledge and complex architectures, LLMs must not be relied upon as the exclusive source of objective truth. Paradoxically, their output may often appear more human-like than we realize, blurring the line between tool and agent.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: “Astonishing” Find: Fossilized Dinosaur Blood in a 115-Million-Year-Old Specimen
content:
Dinosaur blood may have built the fictional Jurassic Park, but coming across it in the real world has proved to be a little more difficult—until now. In a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2614248123) in _Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences_, a team of paleontologists and geochemists announced they’ve struck 115-million-year-old paydirt.

The team found the blood cells in the hind leg bone of a juvenile Cretaceous-era theropod (_Aratasaurus museunacionali_) excavated from a Brazilian mine in 2008. After taking thin slices of the fossilized bones, chemically treating them, and giving them a thorough inspection under an electron microscope, they discovered round blobs roughly the size of cells. The blobs were localized to vascular channels that would have carried blood vessels when the dinosaur was alive.

**Read more: “[We Finally Know Tyrannosaurus Rex’s Body Temperature](https://nautil.us/we-finally-know-tyrannosaurus-rexs-body-temperature-1285067)”**

It was a strong suggestion that the blood cells had fossilized along with the rest of the dinosaur, but to be certain, they performed chemical analyses on both the bones and the surrounding sediment. Within the fossilized bones, they detected the presence of heme—the ring-shaped iron-bearing molecule found in hemoglobin. The non-dinosaur sediment, on the other hand, had none.

“To detect intact heme-derived molecules in 115-million-year-old red blood cells is astonishing: This really is a landmark discovery,” study author Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Australia said in a [statement](https://www.curtin.edu.au/news/media-release/dinosaur-blood-oldest-discovery-rewrites-what-fossils-can-reveal-about-the-past/). “It not only extends the known fossil record of blood, but also offers a direct molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals so we may better understand them and the world they lived in.”

Speaking of physiology, the team compared the shapes of blood cells to those from birds and crocodiles. The dinosaur cells were a little more oblong than the cells from their closest living relatives, but it’s unclear what, if any, conclusions can be drawn. According to the team, it’s possible they were simply deformed during a fossilization process that happened fast enough to preserve the cells in the first place.

Of course, the real highlight of the study isn’t the dinosaur’s blood cells _per se_, it’s that it’s possible for these cells to survive at all. “These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time,” Grice explained. “It opens exciting new avenues for molecular-level palaeontology, allowing us to investigate the evolution of blood, metabolism and even activity levels in ancient animals.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: A Neuropsychologist Explains the Importance of Exercise in Fighting Dementia
content:
Billions of dollars are being spent on research to find a molecule that will cure Alzheimer’s disease. Yet, as Dr. Louis Bherer explains, adopting certain lifestyle habits could significantly reduce the risk of developing symptoms, in some cases by up to half.

Bherer is a professor in the Department of Medicine at the Université de Montréal and researcher and director at the EPIC Centre, the preventive medicine and physical activity center at the Institut de Cardiologie de Montréal (Montreal Heart Institute). His work focuses on the impact of lifestyle, physical exercise and cognitive stimulation on the brain health of older adults and patients with cardiovascular disease.

At his Montréal laboratory, Bherer and his team develop both physical and cognitive exercise programs. The results of their studies corroborate what other research has found on the importance of lifestyle in the prevention of dementia. This factor has been neglected by public health authorities, explains Bherer, who is also laboratory director at the l’Institut universitaire de gériatrie de Montréal (Montreal University Institute of Geriatrics). _The Conversation Canada_ recently spoke to Dr. Bherer.

**[A new Statistics Canada study](https://www.ctvnews.ca/health/article/canadian-women-live-longer-but-spend-more-years-in-poor-health-statcan/) indicates a substantial decline in healthy life expectancy in Canada. In 2023, it was 66.9 years, a decrease of 3.5 years from the peak of 70.4 years between 2010 and 2012. Are you surprised?**

**Bherer:** Yes and no. But what we do know is that the healthspan-lifespan gap — the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy — is widening. For example, nine out of 10 people have at least one risk factor for cardiovascular disease after the age of 65: being overweight, poor sleep, inactivity, high blood pressure, etc. As life expectancy increases, this means more years in poor health.

Our lifestyle is not optimal. Stress and anxiety are on the rise. It’s a scourge. What’s more, people are inactive, they have sleep problems, they are neglecting their diet. We eat quickly, and eat fast food or ultra-processed foods. Although the information is there, and available, we don’t always apply it. Nor do we teach our children to. Physical education should be part of the daily school curriculum, and the basics of nutrition should also be taught.

For that matter, people are quick to turn to pharmaceutical solutions. The popularity of Ozempic is one example. We want to lose weight, but we aren’t addressing the causes of being overweight. We don’t do much to encourage people to change their lifestyle. It is estimated that nearly half of all dementia cases (45 per cent) could be prevented with a healthy lifestyle. [Fourteen modifiable risk factors](https://www.alzint.org/resource/dementia-risk-factors-infographic/) (FRM) have been identified.

**Many people tell themselves: I’m 65 or 70, so it’s too late for me to change my habits. I should have started earlier.**

**Bherer:** It’s [never too late](https://theconversation.com/downsizing-to-an-early-death-why-exercise-is-so-important-as-you-age-123137), even though we know that education (a mitigating factor for dementia) is generally acquired at a young age. This is in contrast to hearing loss, which occurs later in life. Many people do not take it seriously or hide it, yet it’s a factor associated with an increased risk of major cognitive impairment or dementia. And, of course, psychological health plays a major role: a person may be inactive because they feel a little depressed or less motivated, but this increases the risks. We don’t realize that overall health factors are all interrelated. Heart and brain health go hand in hand. What’s good for the heart is good for the brain.

**Your laboratory, which focuses on cognitive health, is located at the Institut de cardiologie de Montréal. What exactly are you doing there?**

****Bherer:**** We use stimulation programs to assess the impact of exercise on physical and cognitive health. Our participants range in age from 50 to 95, with an average age of between 68 and 70. We follow them for periods ranging from three months to a year. They may have mild cognitive deficits that people around them have noticed, and sometimes they suffer from anxiety, a condition that can impact memory and be a predictor of dementia. Other participants have no cognitive issues, but they are at risk due to high blood pressure, diabetes, etc. Our programs include memory games on phones, for example, which improve cognitive function, particularly psycho-motor speed, as well as physical exercises: stationary bikes, treadmills, muscle strengthening, etc. The best approach is a combination of both.

**What have you observed?**

****Bherer:**** We are seeing clinically significant improvements. Participants with mild cognitive impairment may see improvements after six months of training, with differences in their attention, alertness and response speed. They are more alert after just a few weeks. We are also seeing an impact on memory, although this takes longer. Using biomarkers, our research attempts to link the parameters that change, both physically and cognitively, to the effects on the brain. With brain imaging, we can measure improvements in blood flow and brain structures, such as the hippocampus, which plays a key role in memory.

Physical training, which participants do three times a week, stimulates the production of proteins that promote neuroplasticity. When muscles work, they produce and release [myokines](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7288608/) and other [exerkines](https://observatoireprevention.org/en/2023/10/30/exerkines-mediators-of-the-health-benefits-of-exercise/). These molecules play an important role in metabolism, inflammation, bone health and even mood. As we often say, exercise is the miracle pill for overall health.

**Many people make profound changes in their lifestyle, but good intentions don’t always last.**

****Bherer:**** Yes, and that’s a shame, because the positive effects of training disappear within a month or a month and a half. [And the older we get, the faster it happens](https://theconversation.com/how-quickly-do-we-become-unfit-160500). Ideally, you should choose activities that can be easily integrated into your daily routine. I’m thinking of running, for example, which is a very complete exercise, very easy to do, and inexpensive. Brisk walking is also good, but the idea is to work up a bit of a sweat. And supplement that with some exercises to increase muscle strength and others to improve posture and mobility. This is an important factor in maintaining independence as we age. The fear of falling is a concern for many older people. Balance and posture control exercises, such as yoga, can really make a huge difference to the health and lifestyle of older people. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: The Relationship Between Comedy, Democracy, and AI](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/veliz_prophecy.jpg?fit=320%2C486&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/10/13/carissa-veliz-prophecy/)

“Humor, more than anything else in the human make-up, can afford an aloofness and an ability to rise above any situation, even if only for a few seconds,” Viktor Frankl wrote in recalling [the role of humor as a lifeline to sanity and survival in the Holocaust](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/08/19/viktor-frankl-humor-survival/).

Humor is a fundamental human freedom: To laugh is to protect ourselves from all that dehumanizes us — tyranny and transactionalism, captivity and commodification. Humor is also fundamental to free societies, to freedom of thought, to democracy: To laugh together is to harmonize our deepest humanity.

Because humor is the art of surprise, it exists beyond the reach of — and is an antidote to — the artifices of predictive computation we mistake for intelligence.

![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/brownbrothers_TheMarginalian-1.jpg?resize=680%2C489&ssl=1)

In her altogether fantastic [manifesto for breaking free from the prison of predictive technologies](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/10/13/carissa-veliz-prophecy/), Carissa Véliz argues that humor thrives in the same “spaces of indeterminacy” where creativity and innovation also thrive. (“Whatever inspiration is, it’s born from a continuous ‘I don’t know,’” the Polish poet Wisława Szymborska observed in her [magnificent Nobel Prize acceptance speech](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/03/27/wislawa-szymborska-nobel-speech/).) With an eye to the emotional attunement of sharing laughter, Véliz considers the relationship between humor, democracy, and AI:

> Our sense of humor is a dialogue, and when we delegate the conversation to AI, we lose the personal relationship with another human being. Democracy itself is a conversation. If we give up our seat at that table and give it to an AI, we will lose our voice.
> 
> 
> Comedy is not inconsequential for democracy. Comedy sets the tone for freedom. It gives us courage. A documentary about comedy clubs in war-torn Ukraine reminds me that humor is not a luxury; it’s indispensable. “When I went to Sarajevo to a film festival,” Cleese says, “people were talking about the early ’90s, when Yugoslavia was falling apart. Sarajevo is down in a valley, and the Serbs were up in the hills throwing shells down, and telescopic snipers were shooting people crossing the street. And they told me that they had found an underground car park, had turned it into a cinema, and they would show comedies, including Monty Python, and they would laugh. When they came out, an hour and a half later, they felt better. Nothing had improved. But they were better able to deal with their situation.” Comedy can be an ally in our challenge to defy the odds.

Humor, like creativity, works by defying expectation. It is a felicitous violation of the norm. Societies thrive and progress by continually challenging the norm, the given, the status quo. Every revolution, every change in regime, is the story of turning the old order from terrible to laughable.

title: Marianne Moore on the Three Elements of Persuasive Writing
content:
[![Image 1: Marianne Moore on the Three Elements of Persuasive Writing](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/predilections_mariannemoore.jpg?fit=320%2C469&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Predilections-Marianne-Moore/dp/0670572764/?tag=braipick-20)

Several years ago, rummaging through the archives of the Academy of American Poets, I came upon a box labeled “Ballots 1950” — the record of the secret vote by the chancellors the year the Academy’s prestigious fellowship was awarded to E.E. Cummings, [catapulting him into renown](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/07/18/e-e-cummings-academy-of-american-poets/). The voting process is a black box — no one outside the Academy ever finds out who else is in the running and by how much the winner wins.

Leafing through the ballots, one other name appeared over and over, so much so that I was impelled to count.

[Marianne Moore](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/03/10/elizabeth-bishop-efforts-of-affection-a-memoir-of-marianne-moore/) had lost by one vote, never knowing how close she had come. It would be many more years until, at 77, she was finally awarded the fellowship.

Long before that, before she won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award ([sharing a table](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/11/30/rachel-carson-national-book-award-speech/) with Rachel Carson at the ceremony), Moore had set down her views on writing in a series of essays later collected in the out-of-print gem [**_Predilections_**](https://www.amazon.com/Predilections-Marianne-Moore/dp/0670572764/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/185490)). Pulsating through them is a reckoning with the impossible task of the writer — to weave tapestries of truth and meaning from the tenuous thread of words on the ramshackle loom of language.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/MarianneMoore_GeorgePlattLynes.jpg?resize=680%2C841&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Predilections-Marianne-Moore/dp/0670572764/?tag=braipick-20)

Marianne Moore (Photograph: George Platt Lynes)

In an essay titled “Feeling and Precision,” Moore writes:

> Feeling at its deepest — as we all have reason to know — tends to be inarticulable. If it does manage to be articulate, it is likely to seem overcondensed, so that the author is resisted as being enigmatic or disobliging or arrogant.

How we name what we feel is not so much a matter of our writing style as of our style of being, because in order to articulate something we must first apprehend it and we apprehend every smallest thing with the whole person — with the frame of reference that is our entire life, the sum of our experience and memory. When “one of New York’s more painstaking magazines” asked Moore to distill her poetic style into a formula, she fought back the “dictatorial” reflex to quip:

> You don’t devise a rhythm, the rhythm is the person, and the sentence but a radiograph of the personality.

And yet a personality can write with more or less persuasion — that is, write more or less well — depending on what the person brings to the writing. In another essay from the collection, Moore identifies the three psychological elements necessary for persuasive writing: “humility, concentration, and gusto.” A generation after Mark Twain assured his friend Helen Keller when she was accused of plagiarism that [“substantially all ideas are second-hand, consciously and unconsciously drawn from a million outside sources,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/05/10/mark-twain-helen-keller-plagiarism-originality/) she writes:

> Humility… is armor, for it realizes that it is impossible to be original, in the sense of doing something that has never been thought of before. Originality is in any case a by-product of sincerity; that is to say, of feeling that is honest and accordingly rejects anything that might cloud the impression.

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/05/ulysses_paladino1.jpg?w=600&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/27/ulysses-mimmo-paladino/)

Illustration by Mimmo Paladino for [a rare edition of James Joyce’s _Ulysses_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/27/ulysses-mimmo-paladino/)

By “concentration” Moore means a kind of discipline — annealing the essence of the sentiment by cutting away all superfluous explanations, elaborations, and distractions of stylistic posturing, being maximally truthfully in the most minimal way possible. Observing that there is always a “helpless sincerity which precipitates a poem” and that a good poem is always “a concentrate,” she writes:

> Concentration — indispensable to persuasion — may feel to itself crystal clear, yet be through its very compression the opposite… I myself would rather be told too little than too much.

Long before we had the language of extrinsic and intrinsic motivation, of finite and infinite games, Moore uses a lovely word, now dusty, for that peculiar private zeal propelling all creative work with its twin dynamos of discipline and deliverance: “gusto.” Echoing Rachel Carson’s [abiding advice on writing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/08/28/rachel-carson-house-of-life-writing-loneliness/) — “If you write what you yourself sincerely think and feel and are interested in,” she had counseled a young writer, “the chances are very high that you will interest other people as well.” — Moore offers:

> Gusto thrives on freedom, and freedom in art, as in life, is the result of a discipline imposed by ourselves. Moreover, any writer overwhelmingly honest about pleasing himself is almost sure to please others.

She maps the fundamental relationship between the three:

> Humility is an indispensable teacher, enabling concentration to heighten gusto.

When creating in integrity with these three values, it ceases to matter how the work is received because the process of locating and articulating the truth as you feel it, the world as you see it, is its own reward. In what may be the best advice I have encountered on how to orient to your own work, Moore writes:

> There are always objecters, but we must not be sensitive about not being liked or not being printed… The thing is to see the vision and not deny it; or care and admit that we do.

Complement with Walt Whitman on [how to keep criticism from sinking your soul](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/01/03/whitman-emerson-criticism/) and Mary Oliver’s [advice on writing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/04/17/mary-oliver-advice-on-writing/), then savor the moving story of [how Marianne Moore saved a rare tree with a poem](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/08/13/marianne-moore-camperdown-elm/).

# The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: The Generosity of Selfishness: C.S. Lewis on How to Be Interesting](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/cslewis_surprisedbyjoy.jpg?fit=320%2C482&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Surprised-Joy-Shape-Early-Life/dp/0062565435/?tag=braipick-20)

Our lives are defined not by what we have but what we give — on what and whom we spend our energy and time, how we share our material possessions and our mental powers, what we do with our gifts. “Anything you do not give freely and abundantly becomes lost to you,” Annie Dillard wrote in [contemplating the nature of creativity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/28/annie-dillard-writing-the-abundance/). “You open your safe and find ashes.”

Paradoxically, the ability to give hinges on the ability to receive: You must be rested in order to labor, taking the repose it takes to recharge your vital energies; you must be interested in order to be interesting, taking the world in with a greedy curiosity that absorbs its beauty and strangeness in order to metabolize it into meaning.

[C.S. Lewis](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/c-s-lewis/) (November 29, 1898–November 22, 1963) offers a wonderfully counterintuitive perspective on our notions of generosity and our ideas about what it means to be interesting in his memoir [**_Surprised by Joy_**](https://www.amazon.com/Surprised-Joy-Shape-Early-Life/dp/0062565435/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1051096211/)).

![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/CSLewis_TheMarginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C689&ssl=1)

C.S. Lewis

With an eye to [the ideal structure of the creative life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/29/c-s-lewis-schedule/), he writes:

> It is a life almost entirely selfish. Selfish, not self-centred: for in such a life my mind would be directed towards a thousand things, not one of which is myself. The distinction is not unimportant. One of the happiest men and most pleasing companions I have ever known was intensely selfish. On the other hand I have known people capable of real sacrifice whose lives were nevertheless a misery to themselves and to others, because self-concern and self-pity filled all their thoughts. Either condition will destroy the soul in the end. But till the end, give me the man who takes the best of everything (even at my expense) and then talks of other things, rather than the man who serves me and talks of himself, and whose very kindnesses are a continual reproach, a continual demand for pity, gratitude, and admiration.

This is also why, Lewis intimates, the “thrill” of our greatest creative breakthroughs — those revelations that give us back to ourselves, out of which we give our best work to the world — is rooted in “self-forgetfulness”:

> Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else — whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard — does the “thrill” arise.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Shut your mouth; open your eyes and ears. Take in what is there.

Couple with John Steinbeck on [the art of receiving](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/11/21/john-steinbeck-sea-of-cortez-receiving/), then revisit C.S. Lewis on [what we long for in our existential longing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/03/c-s-lewis-longing/).
